title: Ibn al-Haytham
hookLine: who showed that we see because light enters the eye, and tested ideas by experiment

lines: DO THE EYES SEND OUT RAYS?
cards: Blink. Did something go out of your eyes to reach the world, or did the world come in? For a long time, serious thinkers argued that the eye sends out rays, like a lamp, and touches what it sees.
A scholar in Cairo set out to settle it, and a story is told about how he got the time.

He had boasted that he could tame the flooding of the Nile; the caliph called him to do it, and when he saw it couldn't be done, he's said to have pretended to be mad to escape the ruler's anger, and spent a long time shut away, writing.
Whether it happened that way or not, the writing survives. His name was Ibn al-Haytham.

teach.b: His great work is the Book of Optics, Kitab al-Manazir. His answer: we see because light comes from things into the eye, not because the eye sends something out. Look at the sun and your eyes hurt.
That is light coming in. What matters more is how he argued it: he didn't just reason, he set up tests.

teach.h: A DARK ROOM AND SOME LAMPS.
teach.b: Take a dark room with a small hole in one wall, and set several lamps outside it. On the wall inside, a separate spot of light appears for each lamp. Cover one lamp, and its spot vanishes while the others stay.
So light travels in straight lines, and each source sends its own. He had a word for this kind of careful checking: i'tibar. He brought the same honesty to books.
In a work of doubts about the great astronomer Ptolemy, he wrote that the seeker of truth should not simply trust the writings of the ancients, however well-known.
The seeker should question what he reads, test it from every side, and suspect even himself, so he isn't fooled by his own wishes.

Muslim scholars before him had heard the Qur'an call them to look at the sky, the earth, the night and the day, as signs for people who reflect. Ibn al-Haytham looked, and then built a room to check what he saw.

how: Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics argued from experiment that light enters the eye, and his doubts about Ptolemy urged seekers to test even the most respected books.

o: a Nile engineer who built the river's first dam
a Cairo scholar who tested how light reaches the eye
an astronomer who said the eye sends out rays

p: one spot of light for each lamp

s: Ibn al-Haytham argued that the eye sends out rays
he argued the opposite: light comes from things into the eye.
he tested his ideas with a dark room and lamps
cover one lamp, and its spot of light on the wall vanishes.
he said well-known books should simply be trusted
in his doubts about Ptolemy he says the seeker should question them.

games.q: you want to know whether light from different lamps travels separately. what do you do?
o: read what the well-known books say and stop there.
set up lamps outside a dark room with a small hole, and cover them one by one.
games.why: he built the test: each lamp makes its own spot on the wall, and covering one makes its spot vanish.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you're sure of about your day or the people in it: that a coworker doesn't like you, that a task will take forever.
Hold it up like a lamp outside the dark room, ask how you could check it, and suspect yourself a little. If you pray, you can ask God to show you things as they are; if not, just stay curious.

wordCard.voice: Ibn al-Haytham. A scholar in Cairo who showed by experiment that light comes into the eye, and told seekers to question even the ancients, and themselves. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: careful checking, considering by trial. a word Ibn al-Haytham used for testing.

carryVoice: Your line: test it. Question even the ancients, and even your own self. See you tomorrow.
